contrarian.text: The four pages tell three stories. F1 breaks at the China plant on allocation seniority, F3 at the same plant through logic a year earlier, F4 at wire in 2029. F2's cold-head break is a parent exit, which phase 3 put on the trade axis, so it is F4's event; the technicians are the only break that belongs in F2. Every page says the United States hub cannot cover Asia because of a European tender rule, when the true limit is capacity nobody has stated. A fifth, demand-led future breaks no node and earns a watch row only.

customer_market.text: The four pages hold on both axes and the dates are in order. My votes are the China plant in F1 and F3, the cold head in F2 and F4. The correction I bring is at the tender criteria: lateness costs share only when a competitor is still delivering. A listing on wire or cryocoolers, a closed strait, or a sealed class warming up reaches every maker, so committees delay rather than switch. Only F3, where a competitor outside the bloc keeps shipping to Japan and India, moves share. Sourcing can settle it by reading whether competitors share the cold-head and wire sources.

financial.text: The four futures differ on both axes and their dates run in order: F3 stops in 2027, F1 in 2028, F4 in 2029, F2 from 2029 to 2031. F2 is inconsistent only where it borrows a parent exit from F4; on earthquake and outage alone it stands. My votes are N17, N05, N17, N05. What no page carries is the cold-head parent's own balance sheet: what share of its revenue this product is, when its debt matures, and who else would buy it. A board acts on those, not on the OEM's sealed share. Sourcing can read them from public filings before the 2027 sourcing cycle.

foreign_trade_payments.text: Votes: N19 in F1, N05 in F2, N17 in F3, N05 in F4. The futures differ on both axes: a physical margin, a hazard, a rule inside a counterparty's borders, an owner. Dates run in order. Two faults: Macroeconomic's F4 opens with a quarter-long stop at the China plant in 2027, itself a breach; Customer and market's F2 trigger is an F4 cause. The wrong thing: both F4 pages stop the United States plant on a listing, but a producer-country listing delays N16 by licence time and stops only N17. Quality and regulatory confirms.

geopolitical.text: Votes: F1 China plant (N17) on allocation seniority; F2 cold head (N05); F3 China plant (N17) through logic (N10); F4 cold head (N05) through the owner. The four pages differ on both axes and the dates run in order, with F3 earliest in 2027. Two breaks are misfiled: the parent exit belongs in F4, and the storm is shared. The missing point is geopolitical: controls are addressed by destination, so a listing aimed at China strands one plant, not both. Only an owner exit or a ban on all buyers stops both plants at once. Confidence moderate, on the instruments' dated record.

infrastructure.text: Votes: F1 helium cover (N19), F2 cold head (N05), F3 China plant through logic (N17, N10), F4 cold head (N05). The four futures hold on both axes and no date is out of order: F3 stops in 2027, F1 breaks from 2027, F2 and F4 from 2029. My round 2 flood belongs in the shared-break column, not in F2. The missing piece is physical, not political: ramp and test at the United States plant (N21) run on allocated helium and a container cycle sized for one hemisphere, so it could not carry Asia in F3 even with open tenders. Site operations and Logistics can confirm.

labor.text: The four futures differ on both axes and their dates run in order: F3 stops in 2027, F1 breaks from 2027 or the winter of 2028 to 2029, F2 and F4 in 2029. I vote N19 in F1, N20 in F2, N17 in F3 and N05 in F4. One break is misfiled: a cold-head stop by parent exit is F4's story, not F2's. Two things are missing. The export port's labour contract runs out in 2030 and no page watches it. And every page's prevention leans on an 18-month requalification that needs skilled people no one has counted, so 18 months is a floor.

macroeconomic.text: I vote N17 for F1, N05 for F2, N17 through N10 for F3 and N05 for F4. The pages separate cleanly on trade but less on helium, because F2 and F4 end at the same cold head and differ only in whether a price or a rule removes it. Allocation sits in F2, owner exit in F4. Dates are in order. What is missing is the price: every page writes an allocation as a stop and none says what the OEM would pay to stay in the queue for helium or cold heads. That ceiling is a Placeholder for Sourcing.

natural_disasters.text: The four futures differ on both axes and the dates run in the right order, with one exception. F4 absorbs a 2027 China plant stop of a quarter that in fact breaches the 30-day line, so its first break moves to N17 unless logic stock is stated. I vote N19 for F1, N05 for F2, N17 for F3 and N05 for F4. The missing piece is regional correlation: cold heads (N05) and compressors (N06) both come from Japan, and the earthquake every sealed page cites would take both plus the Japan lanes (N29) at once. Every page prices a single-site loss.

security.text: The panel's votes from this lens are N19 in F1, N05 in F2, N17 in F3 and N05 in F4. The pages hold together across both axes, and the stop in F3 lands before the cost in F1 turns into a stop, as it should. What none of them tests is an encrypted carrier. Every shared break is placed at the OEM's plant, the wire mill or the cold-head maker, with the design record assumed intact, yet the incident record in this sector sits with forwarders, terminals and gas carriers. A five-week outage at the helium carriers walks through cover at the US plant with no weather or rule.

technology_shift.text: Votes: F1 helium cover at the United States plant (N19), F2 cold head (N05), F3 China plant through logic (N17, N10), F4 wire (N03). The futures differ on both axes and the dates run in order, F3 stopping first in 2027. One inconsistency: the sealed pages assume a majority by 2029, a one-year diffusion from a 3 tesla clearance, where the 1.5 tesla precedent stayed a minority for eight years. One misplaced break: Customer and market's parent-exit trigger belongs in F4, not F2. No page states the sealed-share curve, which decides whether F2 and F4 exist by 2031.
